claim: Drosophila female germline stem cells (GSCs) have a non-canonical distribution of PRC2 activity.
source: We show that Drosophila female germline stem cells (GSCs) provide a powerful system for studying Polycomb silencing. GSCs have a non-canonical distribution of PRC2 activity and lack silenced chromatin like embryonic progenitors.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIPseq data showing H3K27me3 distribution in GSCs (Figure 2C, 2D, 2H) and immunofluorescence staining (Figure 3A).

claim: Drosophila female germline stem cells lack silenced chromatin like embryonic progenitors.
source: GSCs have a non-canonical distribution of PRC2 activity and lack silenced chromatin like embryonic progenitors.
evidence: This claim is supported by reporter assays showing lack of E(z)-dependent silencing in GSCs (Figure 1G, 1H) and ChIPseq data (Figure 2).

claim: As GSC daughters differentiate into nurse cells and oocytes, nurse cells silence genes in traditional Polycomb domains.
source: As GSC daughters differentiate into nurse cells and oocytes, nurse cells, like embryonic somatic cells, silence genes in traditional Polycomb domains and in generally inactive chromatin.
evidence: This claim is supported by reporter assays showing E(z)-dependent silencing in nurse cells (Figure 1E, 1G, 1H) and ChIPseq data showing H3K27me3 enrichment on PcG domains in nurse cells (Figure 2C, 2D, 2E).

claim: Nurse cells silence genes in generally inactive chromatin.
source: As GSC daughters differentiate into nurse cells and oocytes, nurse cells, like embryonic somatic cells, silence genes in traditional Polycomb domains and in generally inactive chromatin.
evidence: This claim is supported by reporter assays showing E(z)-dependent silencing of reporters in inactive domains (Figure 1G, 1H) and ChIPseq data showing H3K27me3 enrichment on inactive domains (Figure 2C, 2D).

claim: Developmentally controlled expression of Pcl and Scm initiates silencing during nurse cell differentiation.
source: Developmentally controlled expression of two Polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2)-interacting proteins, Pcl and Scm, initiate silencing during differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence showing Pcl depletion and Scm induction during differentiation (Figure 3A), RNAseq data (Figure 3C), and functional experiments showing PclGLKD and ScmGLKD effects on silencing (Figures 5, 6).

claim: In GSCs, abundant Pcl inhibits PRC2-dependent silencing globally.
source: In GSCs, abundant Pcl inhibits PRC2-dependent silencing globally, while in nurse cells Pcl declines and newly induced Scm concentrates PRC2 activity on traditional Polycomb domains.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence showing high Pcl levels in GSCs (Figure 3A), PclGLKD experiments showing ectopic silencing in GSCs (Figure 6C), and ChIPseq data showing altered H3K27me3 distribution after PclGLKD in GSCs (Figure 5D, 5E).

claim: In nurse cells, Pcl declines and newly induced Scm concentrates PRC2 activity on traditional Polycomb domains.
source: In GSCs, abundant Pcl inhibits PRC2-dependent silencing globally, while in nurse cells Pcl declines and newly induced Scm concentrates PRC2 activity on traditional Polycomb domains.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence showing Pcl depletion and Scm induction in nurse cells (Figure 3A), in situ hybridization showing Pcl mRNA localization (Figure 3E), and ChIPseq data showing Scm is required for H3K27me3 enrichment on PcG domains (Figure 5A, 5D, 5E).

claim: PRC2-dependent silencing is developmentally regulated by accessory proteins that either increase the concentration of PRC2 at target sites or inhibit the rate that PRC2 samples chromatin.
source: Our results suggest that PRC2-dependent silencing is developmentally regulated by accessory proteins that either increase the concentration of PRC2 at target sites or inhibit the rate that PRC2 samples chromatin.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data showing Scm concentrates PRC2 on PcG domains (Figure 5) and Pcl inhibits silencing in GSCs (Figure 6), combined with the proposed model (Figure 6D).

claim: Polycomb silencing was initially characterized by genetic studies of Hox gene regulation along the anterior-posterior axis of the Drosophila embryo.
source: Initially characterized by genetic studies of Hox gene regulation along the anterior-posterior axis of the Drosophila embryo (Lewis, 1978), Polycomb group gene (PcG-gene) products recognize repressed loci, coat kilobases of repressed enhancer regions (PcG domains), limit transcription, and restrict eventual cell fates (Schuettengruber et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lewis, 1978 and Schuettengruber et al., 2017.

claim: Polycomb group gene products recognize repressed loci, coat kilobases of repressed enhancer regions (PcG domains), limit transcription, and restrict eventual cell fates.
source: Initially characterized by genetic studies of Hox gene regulation along the anterior-posterior axis of the Drosophila embryo (Lewis, 1978), Polycomb group gene (PcG-gene) products recognize repressed loci, coat kilobases of repressed enhancer regions (PcG domains), limit transcription, and restrict eventual cell fates (Schuettengruber et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Schuettengruber et al., 2017.

claim: Polycomb silencing is utilized by mammalian embryos and likely by all animals.
source: Subsequent research revealed that Polycomb silencing is also utilized by mammalian embryos and likely by all animals, and contributes to the differentiation of all somatic embryonic cells as well as progeny cells downstream from pluripotent embryonic stem cells (ESCs) (Aloia et al., 2013; Montgomery et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Aloia et al., 2013 and Montgomery et al., 2005.

claim: Polycomb silencing contributes to the differentiation of all somatic embryonic cells as well as progeny cells downstream from pluripotent embryonic stem cells.
source: Subsequent research revealed that Polycomb silencing is also utilized by mammalian embryos and likely by all animals, and contributes to the differentiation of all somatic embryonic cells as well as progeny cells downstream from pluripotent embryonic stem cells (ESCs) (Aloia et al., 2013; Montgomery et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Aloia et al., 2013 and Montgomery et al., 2005.

claim: Female germ cells in Drosophila, mouse, and diverse other species give rise to oocytes and mostly produce nurse cells.
source: Female germ cells in Drosophila, mouse, and diverse other species (Lei and Spradling, 2016; Matova and Cooley, 2001), not only give rise to oocytes but also mostly produce a late-differentiating cell type known as nurse cells that nourish the oocytes by donating cytoplasmic organelles, RNAs, and proteins before undergoing programmed cell death.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lei and Spradling, 2016 and Matova and Cooley, 2001.

claim: Nurse cells nourish oocytes by donating cytoplasmic organelles, RNAs, and proteins before undergoing programmed cell death.
source: Female germ cells in Drosophila, mouse, and diverse other species (Lei and Spradling, 2016; Matova and Cooley, 2001), not only give rise to oocytes but also mostly produce a late-differentiating cell type known as nurse cells that nourish the oocytes by donating cytoplasmic organelles, RNAs, and proteins before undergoing programmed cell death.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lei and Spradling, 2016 and Matova and Cooley, 2001.

claim: In Drosophila, germ cells undergo four rounds of synchronous divisions to produce interconnected 16-cell germline cysts.
source: In Drosophila, germ cells undergo four rounds of synchronous divisions to produce interconnected 16-cell germline cysts, which are wrapped by somatic cells to constitute an ovarian follicle.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to de Cuevas and Spradling, 1998.

claim: Germline cysts are wrapped by somatic cells to constitute an ovarian follicle.
source: In Drosophila, germ cells undergo four rounds of synchronous divisions to produce interconnected 16-cell germline cysts, which are wrapped by somatic cells to constitute an ovarian follicle.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to de Cuevas and Spradling, 1998.

claim: The initial cyst cell becomes the oocyte, whereas the other 15 differentiate as nurse cells.
source: The initial cyst cell becomes the oocyte, whereas the other 15 differentiate as nurse cells (de Cuevas and Spradling, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to de Cuevas and Spradling, 1998.

claim: Germline mutation of E(z) and Su(z)12 disrupt nurse cell/oocyte differentiation.
source: Whether nurse cells are true somatic cells that differentiate using canonical Polycomb silencing or whether they remain germ cells is controversial (Figure 1A), because germline mutation of only a few PcG-group genes (E(z) and Su(z)12) disrupt nurse cell/oocyte differentiation while mutation of most others do not (Iovino et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Iovino et al., 2013.

claim: Mutation of most PcG-group genes other than E(z) and Su(z)12 do not disrupt nurse cell/oocyte differentiation.
source: Whether nurse cells are true somatic cells that differentiate using canonical Polycomb silencing or whether they remain germ cells is controversial (Figure 1A), because germline mutation of only a few PcG-group genes (E(z) and Su(z)12) disrupt nurse cell/oocyte differentiation while mutation of most others do not (Iovino et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Iovino et al., 2013.

claim: PRC1 is an E3 ligase that ubiquitylates histone H2A on lysine 119 (H2AK119ub).
source: PcG genes encode two major protein complexes, Polycomb Repressive Complex 1 (PRC1), an E3 ligase that ubiquitylates histone H2A on lysine 119 (H2AK119ub) (Franke et al., 1992; Shao et al., 1999; Wang et al., 2004), and PRC2, which methylates histone H3 on lysine 27 (H3K27me1/2/3) (Cao et al., 2002; Czermin et al., 2002; Kuzmichev et al., 2002; Müller et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Franke et al., 1992; Shao et al., 1999; Wang et al., 2004.

claim: PRC2 methylates histone H3 on lysine 27 (H3K27me1/2/3).
source: PcG genes encode two major protein complexes, Polycomb Repressive Complex 1 (PRC1), an E3 ligase that ubiquitylates histone H2A on lysine 119 (H2AK119ub) (Franke et al., 1992; Shao et al., 1999; Wang et al., 2004), and PRC2, which methylates histone H3 on lysine 27 (H3K27me1/2/3) (Cao et al., 2002; Czermin et al., 2002; Kuzmichev et al., 2002; Müller et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cao et al., 2002; Czermin et al., 2002; Kuzmichev et al., 2002; Müller et al., 2002.

claim: In fly embryos, silencing and PRC2-dependent H3K27me3 enrichment on PcG domains first appears during cell cycle 14.
source: In fly embryos, silencing and PRC2-dependent H3K27me3 enrichment on PcG domains first appears as anterior-posterior patterning is being completed during a massive upregulation of zygotic gene expression during cell cycle 14 (Alhaj Abed et al., 2018; Li et al., 2014; Pelegri and Lehmann, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Alhaj Abed et al., 2018; Li et al., 2014; Pelegri and Lehmann, 1994.

claim: In preimplantation mouse embryos, H3K27me3 is distributed in a 'noncanonical' pattern throughout gene deserts and inactive loci.
source: In preimplantation mouse embryos, H3K27me3 is distributed in a 'noncanonical' pattern throughout gene deserts and inactive loci (Liu et al., 2016; Zheng et al., 2016) and is not further enriched on its canonical sites: CpG-rich 'islands' (CGIs) around enhancers and promoters of developmentally-induced genes (Ku et al., 2008; Tanay et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2016; Zheng et al., 2016.

claim: In preimplantation mouse embryos, H3K27me3 is not further enriched on CpG-rich 'islands' (CGIs) around enhancers and promoters of developmentally-induced genes.
source: In preimplantation mouse embryos, H3K27me3 is distributed in a 'noncanonical' pattern throughout gene deserts and inactive loci (Liu et al., 2016; Zheng et al., 2016) and is not further enriched on its canonical sites: CpG-rich 'islands' (CGIs) around enhancers and promoters of developmentally-induced genes (Ku et al., 2008; Tanay et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ku et al., 2008; Tanay et al., 2007.

claim: H3K27me3 is highly enriched on CGIs in mouse embryonic stem cell cultures derived from preimplantation embryos.
source: However, H3K27me3 is highly enriched on CGIs in mouse embryonic stem cell cultures derived from preimplantation embryos (Boyer et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Boyer et al., 2006.

claim: In flies, Polycomb Response Elements (PREs) embedded within PcG domains recruit the DNA-binding PhoRC complex, PRC1, and PRC2, as well as Scm.
source: In flies, Polycomb Response Elements (PREs) embedded within PcG domains recruit the DNA-binding PhoRC complex, PRC1, and PRC2, as well as Scm, which physically interacts with all three complexes (Brown et al., 1998; Busturia et al., 2001; Fritsch et al., 1999; Kang et al., 2015; Klymenko et al., 2006; Mishra et al., 2001; Shimell et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brown et al., 1998; Busturia et al., 2001; Fritsch et al., 1999; Kang et al., 2015; Klymenko et al., 2006; Mishra et al., 2001; Shimell et al., 2000.

claim: Scm physically interacts with PhoRC, PRC1, and PRC2.
source: In flies, Polycomb Response Elements (PREs) embedded within PcG domains recruit the DNA-binding PhoRC complex, PRC1, and PRC2, as well as Scm, which physically interacts with all three complexes (Brown et al., 1998; Busturia et al., 2001; Fritsch et al., 1999; Kang et al., 2015; Klymenko et al., 2006; Mishra et al., 2001; Shimell et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brown et al., 1998; Busturia et al., 2001; Fritsch et al., 1999; Kang et al., 2015; Klymenko et al., 2006; Mishra et al., 2001; Shimell et al., 2000.

claim: PREs are enriched in several hundred broad H3K27me3-coated loci including the Hox clusters and the enhancers of other developmentally regulated transcription factors and signaling components.
source: PREs are enriched in several hundred broad H3K27me3-coated loci including the Hox clusters and the enhancers of other developmentally regulated transcription factors and signaling components (Schwartz et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Schwartz et al., 2006.

claim: Mammals lack PRE-like sequences.
source: Mammals, however, lack PRE-like sequences and instead enrich PcG proteins on CGIs to silence a larger number of tissue-specific genes than flies (Jermann et al., 2014; Ku et al., 2008; Lynch et al., 2012; Mendenhall et al., 2010; Tanay et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jermann et al., 2014; Ku et al., 2008; Lynch et al., 2012; Mendenhall et al., 2010; Tanay et al., 2007.

claim: Mammals enrich PcG proteins on CGIs to silence a larger number of tissue-specific genes than flies.
source: Mammals, however, lack PRE-like sequences and instead enrich PcG proteins on CGIs to silence a larger number of tissue-specific genes than flies (Jermann et al., 2014; Ku et al., 2008; Lynch et al., 2012; Mendenhall et al., 2010; Tanay et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jermann et al., 2014; Ku et al., 2008; Lynch et al., 2012; Mendenhall et al., 2010; Tanay et al., 2007.

claim: Flies encode Jarid2 and Pcl, homologues of mammalian PRC2 accessory proteins that increase PRC2 activity at CGIs.
source: For example, flies encode Jarid2 and Pcl, homologues of mammalian PRC2 accessory proteins that increase PRC2 activity at CGIs by binding to H2AK119ub, other modified histones, or CGI DNA (Ballaré et al., 2012; Cooper et al., 2016; Healy et al., 2019; Hunkapiller et al., 2012; Højfeldt et al., 2019; Kalb et al., 2014; Li et al., 2010; Li et al., 2017; Perino et al., 2018; Son et al., 2013; Walker et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ballaré et al., 2012; Cooper et al., 2016; Healy et al., 2019; Hunkapiller et al., 2012; Højfeldt et al., 2019; Kalb et al., 2014; Li et al., 2010; Li et al., 2017; Perino et al., 2018; Son et al., 2013; Walker et al., 2010.

claim: Mammalian PRC2 accessory proteins increase PRC2 activity at CGIs by binding to H2AK119ub, other modified histones, or CGI DNA.
source: For example, flies encode Jarid2 and Pcl, homologues of mammalian PRC2 accessory proteins that increase PRC2 activity at CGIs by binding to H2AK119ub, other modified histones, or CGI DNA (Ballaré et al., 2012; Cooper et al., 2016; Healy et al., 2019; Hunkapiller et al., 2012; Højfeldt et al., 2019; Kalb et al., 2014; Li et al., 2010; Li et al., 2017; Perino et al., 2018; Son et al., 2013; Walker et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ballaré et al., 2012; Cooper et al., 2016; Healy et al., 2019; Hunkapiller et al., 2012; Højfeldt et al., 2019; Kalb et al., 2014; Li et al., 2010; Li et al., 2017; Perino et al., 2018; Son et al., 2013; Walker et al., 2010.

claim: H2AK119ub is minimally important for PRC2 targeting in flies.
source: However, H2AK119ub is minimally important for PRC2 targeting in flies (Gutiérrez et al., 2012; Pengelly et al., 2015), and while fly Pcl promotes PRC2 activity on PREs, it lacks DNA-binding site specificity (Choi et al., 2017; Nekrasov et al., 2007; Savla et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gutiérrez et al., 2012; Pengelly et al., 2015.

claim: Fly Pcl promotes PRC2 activity on PREs but lacks DNA-binding site specificity.
source: However, H2AK119ub is minimally important for PRC2 targeting in flies (Gutiérrez et al., 2012; Pengelly et al., 2015), and while fly Pcl promotes PRC2 activity on PREs, it lacks DNA-binding site specificity (Choi et al., 2017; Nekrasov et al., 2007; Savla et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Choi et al., 2017; Nekrasov et al., 2007; Savla et al., 2008.

claim: A reporter integrated near Dak1 was strongly induced in nurse cells following heat shock.
source: The reporter integrated near Dak1 was strongly induced in nurse cells following heat shock, while the reporters integrated near Antp or OR67D did not induce following heat shock.
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Reporters integrated near Antp or OR67D did not induce following heat shock in nurse cells.
source: The reporter integrated near Dak1 was strongly induced in nurse cells following heat shock, while the reporters integrated near Antp or OR67D did not induce following heat shock.
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: E(z)GLKD relieved repression of the reporter near Antp and OR67D but had no effect at Dak1.
source: GermLine-specific RNAi Knock Down (GLKD) of E(z) (E(z)GLKD) relieved repression of the reporter near Antp and OR67D but had no effect at Dak1.
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Reporters in active domains were highly induced while reporters in PcG and inactive domains were nearly uninducible in stage 9–10 nurse cells.
source: In all cases, reporters in active domains were highly induced while reporters in PcG and inactive domains were nearly uninducible in stage 9–10 nurse cells (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative fluorescence data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Very little difference in reporter induction was observed between active and repressed loci in germ cells prior to the onset of meiosis in region 2A.
source: We observed very little difference in reporter induction between active and repressed loci in germ cells prior to the onset of meiosis in region 2A (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative fluorescence data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: By stage 1–2, reporters in all inactive and some PcG domains were less inducible than those in active domains.
source: However, by stage 1–2, reporters in all inactive and some PcG domains were less inducible than those in active domains (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative fluorescence data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: E(z)-dependent reporter silencing was reliably detected in all inactive and most PcG domains by stage 1–2.
source: While reporters in active chromatin were not affected by E(z)GLKD at any stage, we reliably detected E(z)-dependent reporter silencing in all inactive and most PcG domains by stage 1–2, and in all PcG domains by stage 6.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative fluorescence data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: E(z)-dependent reporter silencing was detected in all PcG domains by stage 6.
source: While reporters in active chromatin were not affected by E(z)GLKD at any stage, we reliably detected E(z)-dependent reporter silencing in all inactive and most PcG domains by stage 1–2, and in all PcG domains by stage 6.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative fluorescence data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The difference between E(z)GLKD and control reporter induction in inactive- and PcG-localized reporters generally increased as nurse cell development progressed.
source: The difference between E(z)GLKD and control reporter induction in inactive- and PcG-localized reporters generally increased as nurse cell development progressed, indicating that E(z)-dependent silencing strengthens over time (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative fluorescence data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: PRC2-dependent reporter gene silencing is absent in germline progenitors.
source: We conclude that PRC2-dependent reporter gene silencing is absent in germline progenitors, initiates in both inactive and PcG domains in nurse cells after germline progenitors differentiate into nurse cells or oocytes, and strengthens as nurse cells grow.
evidence: This claim is based on reporter assay data shown in Figures 1G and 1H.

claim: PRC2-dependent reporter gene silencing initiates in both inactive and PcG domains in nurse cells after germline progenitors differentiate into nurse cells or oocytes.
source: We conclude that PRC2-dependent reporter gene silencing is absent in germline progenitors, initiates in both inactive and PcG domains in nurse cells after germline progenitors differentiate into nurse cells or oocytes, and strengthens as nurse cells grow.
evidence: This claim is based on reporter assay data shown in Figures 1G and 1H.

claim: PRC2-dependent reporter gene silencing strengthens as nurse cells grow.
source: We conclude that PRC2-dependent reporter gene silencing is absent in germline progenitors, initiates in both inactive and PcG domains in nurse cells after germline progenitors differentiate into nurse cells or oocytes, and strengthens as nurse cells grow.
evidence: This claim is based on reporter assay data shown in Figures 1G and 1H.

claim: H3K27me3 was highly enriched on PcG domains in nurse cell nuclei from late stages.
source: We analyzed chromatin from purified nurse cell nuclei from late stages well after repression was complete (512c, stage 9–10), and found that H3K27me3 was highly enriched on PcG domains.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIPseq data shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: Lower but significant H3K27me3 enrichment occurred on Inactive domains in nurse cells.
source: Moreover, lower but significant H3K27me3 enrichment occurred on Inactive domains, which were co-enriched for H3K27me2 (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIPseq data shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: Inactive domains were co-enriched for H3K27me2 in nurse cells.
source: Moreover, lower but significant H3K27me3 enrichment occurred on Inactive domains, which were co-enriched for H3K27me2 (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIPseq data shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: Predominantly mitotic (2c) or differentiated (16c) somatic follicle cell nuclei contained a similar H3K27me3 distribution as nurse cells.
source: Predominantly mitotic (2c) or differentiated (16c) somatic follicle cell nuclei contained a similar H3K27me3 distribution as nurse cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIPseq data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 117 out of 118 PcG domains were highly enriched for H3K27me3 in nurse cells.
source: When we measured H3K27me3 enrichment on all 118 PcG domains from Kharchenko et al., 2011, 117 and 112 were highly enriched for H3K27me3 in nurse cells and follicle cells, respectively (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIPseq data shown in Figure 2E and 2F.

claim: 112 out of 118 PcG domains were highly enriched for H3K27me3 in follicle cells.
source: When we measured H3K27me3 enrichment on all 118 PcG domains from Kharchenko et al., 2011, 117 and 112 were highly enriched for H3K27me3 in nurse cells and follicle cells, respectively (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIPseq data shown in Figure 2E and 2F.

claim: Genes located within PcG domains that were depleted for H3K27me3 in nurse or follicle cells (fusilli, eyes absent, tramtrack, 18 wheeler, and apontic) had known expression and functions in oogenesis.
source: Genes located within PcG domains that were depleted for H3K27me3 in nurse or follicle cells (fusilli, eyes absent, tramtrack, 18 wheeler, and apontic) had known expression and functions in oogenesis (Figure 2E, Table 1; Bai and Montell, 2002; French et al., 2003; Kleve et al., 2006; Lie and Macdonald, 1999; Starz-Gaiano et al., 2008; Wakabayashi-Ito et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIPseq data (Figure 2E, Table 1) and citations to Bai and Montell, 2002; French et al., 2003; Kleve et al., 2006; Lie and Macdonald, 1999; Starz-Gaiano et al., 2008; Wakabayashi-Ito et al., 2001.

claim: Nurse cells and follicle cells each contained seven additional H3K27me3-enriched domains that were annotated as either active domains (6) or inactive domains (1) in S2 cells.
source: Through manual curating, we also found that nurse cells and follicle cells each contained seven additional H3K27me3-enriched domains (two shared) that were annotated as either active domains (6) or inactive domains (1) in S2 cells (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIPseq data analysis and Table 1.

claim: 111 out of 130 PcG domains (85%) were shared between nurse cells, follicle cells, and S2 cells.
source: In total, 111 out of 130 PcG domains (85%) were shared between all three cell types (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIPseq data analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Nurse cells contain a highly similar collection of H3K27me3-enriched PcG domains as somatic cells.
source: We conclude that nurse cells contain a highly similar collection of H3K27me3-enriched PcG domains as somatic cells, and that only a few PcG domains differ between nurse cells and other somatic cells.
evidence: This claim is based on ChIPseq data analysis shown in Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: Only a few PcG domains differ between nurse cells and other somatic cells.
source: We conclude that nurse cells contain a highly similar collection of H3K27me3-enriched PcG domains as somatic cells, and that only a few PcG domains differ between nurse cells and other somatic cells.
evidence: This claim is based on ChIPseq data analysis shown in Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: GSCs did not highly enrich H3K27me3 on PcG domains.
source: We observed a 'non-canonical' H3K27me3 distribution in Drosophila GSCs that is similar to that observed in early embryos (Figure 2C). In contrast to the canonical H3K27me3 distribution in nurse cells, GSCs did not highly enrich H3K27me3 on PcG domains.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIPseq data shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: GSCs had similar amounts of total H3K27me3 signal as nurse cells or follicle cells relative to spike-in.
source: Relative to spike-in, GSCs had similar amounts of total H3K27me3 signal as nurse cells or follicle cells, but the signal was more evenly distributed across the genome (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by spike-in normalized ChIPseq data shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: H3K27me3 signal in GSCs was more evenly distributed across the genome compared to nurse cells or follicle cells.
source: Relative to spike-in, GSCs had similar amounts of total H3K27me3 signal as nurse cells or follicle cells, but the signal was more evenly distributed across the genome (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by spike-in normalized ChIPseq data shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: In GSCs, there was no greater enrichment of H3K27me3 on PcG domains compared to generally inactive domains.
source: In GSCs, we noted no greater enrichment of H3K27me3 on PcG domains compared to generally inactive domains in contrast to an approximately 10-fold enrichment in late stage nurse cells or follicle cells (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIPseq data analysis shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Late stage nurse cells or follicle cells showed approximately 10-fold enrichment of H3K27me3 on PcG domains compared to inactive domains.
source: In GSCs, we noted no greater enrichment of H3K27me3 on PcG domains compared to generally inactive domains in contrast to an approximately 10-fold enrichment in late stage nurse cells or follicle cells (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIPseq data analysis shown in Figure 2H.

claim: H3K27me3 signal in GSCs was depleted from S2 cell active domains.
source: H3K27me3 signal in GSCs was depleted from S2 cell active domains (Figure 2H), or more specifically, genes with H3K27ac, a transcription-promoting modification, near their transcription start sites (TSSs) (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIPseq data analysis shown in Figure 2H and 2G.

claim: H3K27me3 signal in GSCs was depleted from genes with H3K27ac near their transcription start sites.
source: H3K27me3 signal in GSCs was depleted from S2 cell active domains (Figure 2H), or more specifically, genes with H3K27ac, a transcription-promoting modification, near their transcription start sites (TSSs) (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIPseq data analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Early embryos (cycle 13) have a non-canonical H3K27me3 distribution that transforms into a canonical distribution in cycle 14.
source: Using published data from Li et al., 2014, we noted a similar depletion of H3K27me3 enrichment from active domains in early embryos and a non-canonical H3K27me3 distribution in cycle 13 embryos that transforms into a canonical distribution in cycle 14 (Figure 2I).
evidence: This claim is supported by reanalysis of published ChIPseq data from Li et al., 2014, shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The process of nurse cell differentiation resembles somatic cell differentiation in early embryos.
source: These experiments show that the process of nurse cell differentiation resembles somatic cell differentiation in early embryos and includes changes in the production of H3K27me3 that transform its broad distribution across non-expressed chromatin into a highly focused pattern on common PcG domains.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of ChIPseq data from GSCs, nurse cells, and embryos (Figures 2C, 2H, 2I).

claim: Nurse cell differentiation includes changes in the production of H3K27me3 that transform its broad distribution across non-expressed chromatin into a highly focused pattern on common PcG domains.
source: These experiments show that the process of nurse cell differentiation resembles somatic cell differentiation in early embryos and includes changes in the production of H3K27me3 that transform its broad distribution across non-expressed chromatin into a highly focused pattern on common PcG domains.

claim: Pcl inhibits silencing by reducing the number of PRC2-chromatin binding events per unit time by increasing the residence time of PRC2 on chromatin with each binding event.
source: Instead, we propose that Pcl inhibits silencing by reducing the number of PRC2-chomatin binding events per unit time by increasing the residence time of PRC2 on chromatin with each binding event (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is a proposed model based on inference from experimental data (Figures 5 and 6) and the model diagram (Figure 6D).

claim: In both flies and mammals, PRC2 transiently associates with chromatin to mono- and dimethylate H3K27 outside of traditional PcG domains, blocking H3K27 acetylation and antagonizing transcription.
source: In both flies and mammals, PRC2 transiently associates with chromatin to mono- and dimethylate H3K27 outside of traditional PcG domains, blocking H3K27 acetylation and antagonizing transcription (Ferrari et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ferrari et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2015.

claim: Strong and widespread PRC2-dependent silencing was found in H3K27me1/2 enriched chromatin in nurse cells.
source: We similarly found strong and widespread PRC2-dependent silencing in H3K27me1/2 enriched chromatin in nurse cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by reporter assay data (Figure 1) and RNAseq data (Figure 7).

claim: Core-PRC2, but not Pcl-PRC2 or H3K27me3, primarily silences inactive chromatin.
source: Because inactive domain silencing was not affected by depletion of Pcl, Jarid2, or H3K27me3 (Figure 7A,B), we propose that core-PRC2, but not Pcl-PRC2 or H3K27me3, primarily silences inactive chromatin (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is a proposed model based on RNAseq data (Figure 7A, B) and the model diagram (Figure 6D).

claim: In GSCs, abundant Pcl could saturate PRC2, effectively depleting faster-sampling core-PRC2 complexes in favor of slower sampling Pcl-PRC2.
source: In GSCs, abundant Pcl could saturate PRC2, effectively depleting faster-sampling core-PRC2 complexes in favor of slower sampling Pcl-PRC2.
evidence: This claim is a proposed model based on inference from experimental data showing high Pcl levels in GSCs (Figure 3A) and the effects of PclGLKD (Figures 5 and 6).

claim: In somatic embryonic cells, Pcl is present in a small fraction of PRC2 complexes.
source: In somatic embryonic cells, Pcl is present in a small fraction of PRC2 complexes (Nekrasov et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nekrasov et al., 2007.

claim: Compared to other fly tissues, Pcl mRNA is most abundant in the ovary.
source: Compared to other fly tissues, Pcl mRNA is most abundant in the ovary (Leader et al., 2018), and within the ovary, Pcl protein is much more abundant in GSCs and nurse cell precursors than differentiated nurse cells and somatic cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Leader et al., 2018.

claim: Within the ovary, Pcl protein is much more abundant in GSCs and nurse cell precursors than differentiated nurse cells and somatic cells.
source: Compared to other fly tissues, Pcl mRNA is most abundant in the ovary (Leader et al., 2018), and within the ovary, Pcl protein is much more abundant in GSCs and nurse cell precursors than differentiated nurse cells and somatic cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Pcl protein levels may be regulated by an mRNA transport mechanism induced in region 2 that also triggers the differentiation of oocytes from nurse cells.
source: Within each differentiated germline cyst, Pcl mRNA is depleted from nurse cells and enriched in oocytes (Figure 3E), suggesting that Pcl protein levels may be regulated by an mRNA transport mechanism induced in region 2 that also triggers the differentiation of oocytes from nurse cells (Huynh and St Johnston, 2000).
evidence: This claim is a suggestion based on in situ hybridization data (Figure 3E) and citation to Huynh and St Johnston, 2000.

claim: Pcl depletion frees core-PRC2 to rapidly sample and silence inactive domains during nurse cell differentiation.
source: During nurse cell differentiation, we propose that Pcl depletion frees core-PRC2 to rapidly sample and silence inactive domains, while Scm (which is absent from the GSC) induction recruits high levels of PRC1 and PRC2 activity around PREs (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is a proposed model based on experimental data (Figures 3, 5, 6) and the model diagram (Figure 6D).

claim: Scm induction recruits high levels of PRC1 and PRC2 activity around PREs during nurse cell differentiation.
source: During nurse cell differentiation, we propose that Pcl depletion frees core-PRC2 to rapidly sample and silence inactive domains, while Scm (which is absent from the GSC) induction recruits high levels of PRC1 and PRC2 activity around PREs (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is a proposed model based on experimental data (Figures 3, 4, 5) and the model diagram (Figure 6D).

claim: ScmGLKD nurse cell chromatin retained a noncanonical H3K27me3 pattern characteristic of GSCs, as if differentiation at PcG domains had not occurred.
source: ScmGLKD nurse cell chromatin retained a noncanonical H3K27me3 pattern characteristic of GSCs, as if differentiation at PcG domains had not occurred (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIPseq data analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: In mice, Scm homologue, Scml2, associates with PcG domains to recruit PRC1/2 and silence PcG targets during male germline development.
source: In mice, Scm homologue, Scml2, similarly associates with PcG domains to recruit PRC1/2 and silence PcG targets during male germline development (Hasegawa et al., 2015; Maezawa et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hasegawa et al., 2015; Maezawa et al., 2018.

claim: Mammalian PGCs partially enrich PRC2 activity on CGIs while fly female GSCs do not enrich PRC2 on specific sites.
source: This difference could explain why mammalian PGCs partially enrich PRC2 activity on CGIs (Lesch et al., 2013; Zheng et al., 2016) while fly female GSCs do not enrich PRC2 on specific sites.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of data from this study (Figure 2) and citations to Lesch et al., 2013; Zheng et al., 2016.

claim: While PcG domain-associated Scm is sufficient to enrich PRC2 activity above background levels found throughout inactive chromatin, Pcl is additionally required to promote full PRC2 and H3K27me3 enrichment on PcG domains.
source: While PcG domain-associated Scm is sufficient to enrich PRC2 activity above background levels found throughout inactive chromatin, a second PRC2 interacting protein, Pcl, is additionally required to promote full PRC2 and H3K27me3 enrichment on PcG domains (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5.

claim: Scm oligomerizes and interacts with PRC2 in vitro.
source: Because Scm oligomerizes and interacts with PRC2 in vitro (Kang et al., 2015; Peterson et al., 1997), it could form an array of PRC2 binding sites anchored to PREs through Sfmbt (Alfieri et al., 2013; Frey et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kang et al., 2015; Peterson et al., 1997.

claim: Scm could form an array of PRC2 binding sites anchored to PREs through Sfmbt.
source: Because Scm oligomerizes and interacts with PRC2 in vitro (Kang et al., 2015; Peterson et al., 1997), it could form an array of PRC2 binding sites anchored to PREs through Sfmbt (Alfieri et al., 2013; Frey et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is a proposed model based on citations to Kang et al., 2015; Peterson et al., 1997; Alfieri et al., 2013; Frey et al., 2016.

claim: Two cooperative interactions, PRC2 with PRE-tethered Scm, and Pcl with DNA, preferentially concentrate H3K27me3-generating Pcl-PRC2 versus H3K27me1/2-generating core-PRC2 on PcG domains.
source: We propose that two cooperative interactions, PRC2 with PRE-tethered Scm, and Pcl with DNA, preferentially concentrate H3K27me3-generating Pcl-PRC2 versus H3K27me1/2-generating core-PRC2 on PcG domains (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is a proposed model based on experimental data (Figures 3, 4, 5) and the model diagram (Figure 6D).

claim: H3K27me3 could be further enriched by H3K27me3-induced allosteric PRC2 activation through the Esc subunit.
source: H3K27me3 could then be further enriched by H3K27me3-induced allosteric PRC2 activation through the Esc subunit (Margueron et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is a proposed mechanism based on citation to Margueron et al., 2009.
